def-csm-frontier-two-velocity-scaling.definition_interface:
Fix a period $L>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T_L:=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$. A smooth periodic function on $\mathbb T_L$ means an $L$-periodic $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R$. For a periodic measurable function $g$ with $\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx<\infty$, use the normalized spatial measure $dm_L=dx/L$ on a period and write

$$\|g\|_{2,L}^2:=\frac1L\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx.$$

Elements of $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C)$ are equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define the wave number $\kappa_n:=2\pi n/L$, character $e_n(x):=\exp(i\kappa_n x)$, and Fourier coefficient $\widehat g(n):=L^{-1}\int_0^L g(x)e^{-i\kappa_nx}\,dx$. These formulas are independent of the chosen representative of $x$ in $\mathbb T_L$.

Let $c>0$ be a speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\lambda>0$ be a switching-rate parameter in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. For smooth real initial data $f_{+,0},f_{-,0}$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the two-velocity periodic model is the linear Cauchy problem below; when these functions represent physical densities, also require $f_{\pm,0}\ge0$.

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}.$$

Here $x\in\mathbb T_L$, $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds, and $f_\pm$ have the units of a linear number density, $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The speed magnitude is $c/\epsilon$, and from either velocity state the rate of switching to the opposite state is $\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Define the total density $\rho^\epsilon:=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$, the flux $j^\epsilon:=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$, and the total mass $M^\epsilon(t):=\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$.

def-csm-frontier-boltzmann-grad-scaling.definition_interface:
Fix an integer dimension $d\ge2$, a period length $L>0$ metres, and an equal particle mass $m>0$ kilograms. The position space is the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$. For lifts $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ of points $[x],[y]\in\mathbb T_L^d$, define

$$\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}([x],[y]):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}|x-y+Lk|,$$

where $|z|=(\sum_{\ell=1}^d z_\ell^2)^{1/2}$ is the Euclidean norm. For $q_i=[x]$ and $q_j=[y]$, the vectors $x-y+Lk$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, are the displacement representatives from $q_j$ to $q_i$. The minimum is attained because $|x-y+Lk|\to\infty$ as $|k|\to\infty$, and its value is independent of the chosen lifts because changing lifts reindexes $k$. For each $N\ge2$ under consideration, let $\delta_N>0$ be the physical sphere diameter in metres and put $a_N:=\delta_N/L$. An admissible configuration $(q_1,\ldots,q_N)$ has pairwise distances $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i,q_j)>\delta_N$. For a hard-sphere trajectory below, require $\delta_N<L/2$; this restriction holds eventually in the scaling prescription. If two quotient displacement representatives of length $\delta_N$ existed, their difference would be a nonzero vector in $L\mathbb Z^d$, of length at least $L$, but the triangle inequality bounds its length by $2\delta_N<L$; thus the contact normal is unique.

A hard-sphere trajectory, when defined, is specified on one interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with time $t\in I$ measured in seconds. For each $i=1,\ldots,N$ its maps are
$$q_i:I\longrightarrow\mathbb T_L^d,\qquad v_i:I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,$$
where $v_i$ is measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Require $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t),q_j(t))\ge\delta_N$ for every $t\in I$ and $i\ne j$. The interval may be bounded or unbounded and may include either finite endpoint. Positions are continuous on $I$. Define the interior contact-time set

$$C:=\{t\in I^\circ:\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t),q_j(t))=\delta_N\text{ for some }i<j\}.$$

Require $C$ to be locally finite in $I^\circ$: every compact interval $[a,b]\subset I^\circ$ contains only finitely many elements of $C$. Each $t_c\in C$ must be a binary contact as defined below. In particular, there is an $\eta>0$ with $(t_c-\eta,t_c+\eta)\subset I^\circ$ and $C\cap(t_c-\eta,t_c+\eta)=\{t_c\}$; this is the meaning of an isolated contact. All pairwise distances are strictly greater than $\delta_N$ at interior times outside $C$. A free-flight interval is a maximal open subinterval of $I^\circ$ containing no point of $C$. On each such interval require every $q_i$ and $v_i$ to be $C^1$ and to satisfy $\dot q_i=v_i$ and $\dot v_i=0$. Here $\dot q_i=v_i$ means that any local Euclidean lift of $q_i$ has derivative $v_i$; changing that lift by a constant lattice vector leaves the derivative unchanged.

At an interior contact time use both one-sided velocity limits and set $v_i(t_c)=v_i^+$, the outgoing value. A finite endpoint is included only when the corresponding limits from within $I$ exist, and the position and velocity maps take those values there. No collision rule involving a missing side of an endpoint is imposed; a two-sided update there would require an extension of the trajectory through that time. Contact times may accumulate only at endpoints of $I$ or at infinity; included finite endpoints still require the stated one-sided limits. These conventions specify a partial trajectory only and assert no continuation through a collision accumulation. A binary contact of particles $i,j$ at an interior time $t_c\in I^\circ$ means $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t_c),q_j(t_c))=\delta_N$, while no other pair is in contact at $t_c$. Write $v_i^-$ and $v_i^+$ for the one-sided velocity limits at the contact. Let $n$ be the unique unit vector from the centre of $j$ to the centre of $i$ along the shortest quotient displacement. All particles other than $i,j$ retain their velocities at this contact. The equal-mass elastic reflection rule is

$$v_i^+=v_i^- -\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n,\qquad v_j^+=v_j^- +\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n.$$

The Boltzmann–Grad scaling prescription is a sequence, indexed by all sufficiently large integers $N$, with $N\to\infty$, $a_N\to0$, and

$$N a_N^{d-1}=\kappa$$

for a fixed dimensionless $\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Under this exact relation, $a_N=(\kappa/N)^{1/(d-1)}\to0$, so the trajectory restriction $\delta_N<L/2$ holds for every sufficiently large $N$. The factor $a_N$ is the diameter measured relative to the fixed box length, so the displayed parameter is dimensionless. This is a definition of a finite hard-sphere model and a scaling prescription only; it asserts neither global existence of the hard-sphere flow nor convergence to a Boltzmann equation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a period $L>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T_L:=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$. A smooth periodic function on $\mathbb T_L$ means an $L$-periodic $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R$. For a periodic measurable function $g$ with $\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx<\infty$, use the normalized spatial measure $dm_L=dx/L$ on a period and write

$$\|g\|_{2,L}^2:=\frac1L\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx.$$

Elements of $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C)$ are equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define the wave number $\kappa_n:=2\pi n/L$, character $e_n(x):=\exp(i\kappa_n x)$, and Fourier coefficient $\widehat g(n):=L^{-1}\int_0^L g(x)e^{-i\kappa_nx}\,dx$. These formulas are independent of the chosen representative of $x$ in $\mathbb T_L$.

Let $c>0$ be a speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\lambda>0$ be a switching-rate parameter in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. For smooth real initial data $f_{+,0},f_{-,0}$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the two-velocity periodic model is the linear Cauchy problem below; when these functions represent physical densities, also require $f_{\pm,0}\ge0$.

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}.$$

Here $x\in\mathbb T_L$, $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds, and $f_\pm$ have the units of a linear number density, $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The speed magnitude is $c/\epsilon$, and from either velocity state the rate of switching to the opposite state is $\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Define the total density $\rho^\epsilon:=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$, the flux $j^\epsilon:=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$, and the total mass $M^\epsilon(t):=\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

derivations.claim: For each $n\in\mathbb Z$, set $v=c/\epsilon$, $\alpha=\lambda/\epsilon^2$, $M_n=\begin{pmatrix}-i\kappa_n v-\alpha&\alpha\\ \alpha&i\kappa_n v-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, and $U_n(0)=(\widehat f_{+,0}(n),\widehat f_{-,0}(n))^{\mathsf T}$. Realify $z\in\mathbb C^2$ by $\mathcal Rz=(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_2)\in\mathbb R^4$, and for $M=P+iQ$ put $\mathcal RM=\begin{pmatrix}P&-Q\\Q&P\end{pmatrix}$. Direct coordinate multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Mz)=(\mathcal RM)\mathcal Rz$ and $|\mathcal Rz|_2^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$. By [F6], $\mathbb R^4$ is Banach; [F7] applied to each row bounds every real $4\times4$ matrix as an operator, and [F8]–[F9] specify the Euclidean and operator norms. By [F5], $\mathcal RU_n(t):=e^{t\mathcal RM_n}\mathcal RU_n(0)$ defines a solution of the realified mode IVP for all $t\ge0$, and pulling back by $\mathcal R$ defines $U_n(t)$. The matrix-valued ODE supplier [F4] gives uniqueness of this vector solution on each compact interval $[0,T]$: embed any vector solution as the first column of a $4\times4$ matrix solution with the other columns zero, and apply [F4]. For any smooth solution of the PDE, integration by parts in real and imaginary parts separately, using [F3], gives these same Fourier mode equations, so the constructed modes are the only possible ones. Define the candidate pair by the Fourier series $F^\epsilon(t,x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}U_n(t)e_n(x)$, with $e_n$ from [F1]. Since real initial data satisfy $U_{-n}(0)=\overline{U_n(0)}$ and $M_{-n}=\overline{M_n}$, uniqueness gives $U_{-n}(t)=\overline{U_n(t)}$, so this series is real. The skew-Hermitian transport part contributes zero to the derivative of $|U_n|^2$, and direct multiplication of the collision matrix gives $(|U_n|^2)'=-2\alpha|\widehat f_+^\epsilon(n,t)-\widehat f_-^\epsilon(n,t)|^2\le0$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and $q>r+1$, periodicity and [F3] give $\widehat{\partial_x^q f_{\pm,0}}(n)=(i\kappa_n)^q\widehat f_{\pm,0}(n)$ by repeated integration by parts; hence $|\widehat f_{\pm,0}(n)|\le |\kappa_n|^{-q}\int_0^L|\partial_x^qf_{\pm,0}(x)|\,dm_L(x)$ for $n\ne0$. Grouping $2^j\le |n|<2^{j+1}$ then shows $\sum_n(1+|\kappa_n|)^r|U_n(0)|<\infty$. The mode bound $|U_n(t)|\le|U_n(0)|$ and $|M_n|=O(1+|n|)$ imply absolute uniform convergence on every compact time interval of the Fourier series and of each differentiated series, since each space derivative contributes a factor $i\kappa_n$ and each time derivative a factor $M_n$. Fourier orthonormality [F2] gives the series coefficients $U_n$; their mode equations and the uniformly convergent differentiated series then verify the PDE termwise. At $t=0$ the series agrees with the prescribed smooth data by Fourier completeness [F2], first in $L^2$ and hence pointwise by continuity. Thus it is a global smooth solution of the Cauchy problem. Any other smooth solution has the same mode equations and initial coefficients; [A1] and [F2] make the solutions equal as $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C^2)$ classes, hence almost everywhere. Both solutions are smooth and therefore continuous in $x$. If their difference were nonzero at some $x_0$, continuity would give a nonempty open arc on which its norm is bounded below by a positive constant; every nonempty open arc has positive normalized Lebesgue measure $dm_L$, contradicting equality almost everywhere. Thus they agree pointwise on $\mathbb T_L$.

Put $F_0=(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$. For $h\ge0$, free transport $T_h(g_+,g_-):=(g_+(\cdot-vh),g_-(\cdot+vh))$ preserves nonnegativity and pair norm. It preserves each component mass because a change of variable turns its integral into an integral of a smooth periodic function over another full period, which is unchanged by [F3]. The pointwise collision operator $C_h$ is the matrix $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+e^{-2\alpha h}&1-e^{-2\alpha h}\\1-e^{-2\alpha h}&1+e^{-2\alpha h}\end{pmatrix}$. Its entries are nonnegative and its column sums are one. The orthonormal vectors $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ have eigenvalues $1$ and $e^{-2\alpha h}\in[0,1]$, so $C_h$ preserves nonnegativity and total mass and contracts the pair norm pointwise, hence in pair $L^2$. Thus the alternating products $(T_{t/m}C_{t/m})^mF_0$ are nonnegative when $F_0$ is and are $L^2$ contractions.

Fix a Fourier mode $k\in\mathbb Z$ and let $A_k=\operatorname{diag}(-i\kappa_kv,i\kappa_kv)$ and $B=\alpha\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Under the realification of step 1.1, their generators are real $4\times4$ matrices $\widetilde A_k=\mathcal R(A_k)$ and $\widetilde B=\mathcal R(B)$. Transport on this mode is $e^{\widetilde A_kh}$, and collision is $e^{\widetilde Bh}$ because the eigenvectors and eigenvalues in step 1.2 diagonalize $B$. By [F6], $\mathbb R^4$ with its Euclidean norm is Banach; applying [F7] rowwise bounds every real matrix as an operator, and [F8]–[F9] give the Euclidean and operator norms used in [F5]. For $X\in\{\widetilde A_k,\widetilde B,\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B\}$, [F5] gives $e^{Xh}=I+hX+R_X(h)$ with $\|R_X(h)\|\le K_Xh^2$ on $0\le h\le t$, where $K_X:=\tfrac12\|X\|^2e^{t\|X\|}$. Multiplying the first two expansions and subtracting the third shows $\|e^{\widetilde A_kh}e^{\widetilde Bh}-e^{(\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B)h}\|\le C_{k,\epsilon,t}h^2$, where one may take $C_{k,\epsilon,t}=\|\widetilde A_k\|\|\widetilde B\|+K_{\widetilde A_k}+K_{\widetilde B}+K_{\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B}+t(\|\widetilde A_k\|K_{\widetilde B}+\|\widetilde B\|K_{\widetilde A_k})+t^2K_{\widetilde A_k}K_{\widetilde B}$. All factors are contractions: the split factors by step 1.2, and the exact mode evolution by the energy identity in step 1.1. Telescoping the $m$-fold products with $h=t/m$ bounds the error by $mC_{k,\epsilon,t}(t/m)^2=C_{k,\epsilon,t}t^2/m$, so the split evolution converges to the exact solution in each fixed mode.

The zero mode in the equations of [F1] satisfies $(\widehat f_+(0)+\widehat f_-(0))'=0$, since the switching terms cancel and the transport frequency is zero. As $M^\epsilon(t)=L(\widehat f_+^\epsilon(0,t)+\widehat f_-^\epsilon(0,t))$, this proves total-mass conservation.

For a finite set of modes, step 2.1 gives convergence of the split evolution to the exact solution. Let $P_{>K}$ be the Fourier projection onto $|k|>K$, applied componentwise. Its initial pair tail tends to zero by [A1] and [F2]. Every split product preserves modes and contracts this tail by step 1.2. The exact evolution also preserves modes; applying the mode energy identity in step 1.1 and summing by Parseval [F2] shows it contracts the same tail. Hence the split products converge in pair $L^2$ to the solution from step 1.1.

The nonnegative cone is closed in real $L^2$: if classes $g_m$ have nonnegative representatives almost everywhere and $g_m\to g$, then for representatives of $g$ and $g_m$ the inequality $g^-\le|g-g_m|$ holds almost everywhere, so $\|g^-\|_2\le\|g-g_m\|_2\to0$. Applying this componentwise, the split products are nonnegative by step 1.2 and converge by step 3.1, so each component of the exact solution is nonnegative almost everywhere. Fix $t\ge0$. Step 1.1 gives smooth, hence continuous, functions $x\mapsto f_\pm^\epsilon(x,t)$. If either component were negative at some $x_0$, continuity would give a nonempty open arc on which it is bounded above by a negative constant. Such an arc has positive $dm_L$ measure, contradicting nonnegativity almost everywhere. Thus both components are nonnegative pointwise for every $t\ge0$.

Under [A1], apply the mode identity in step 1.1 to the difference of two solutions; summing over $n$ by Parseval [F2] gives the stated contraction. Step 1.1 gives uniform convergence of the solution and time-derivative Fourier series, so termwise differentiation of Parseval's sum is valid. Applying the same sum to one solution gives $\frac{d}{dt}\|F^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2=-2\alpha\|f_+^\epsilon(t)-f_-^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2$, which is the displayed dissipation identity because $\alpha=\lambda/\epsilon^2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a period $L>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T_L:=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$. A smooth periodic function on $\mathbb T_L$ means an $L$-periodic $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R$. For a periodic measurable function $g$ with $\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx<\infty$, use the normalized spatial measure $dm_L=dx/L$ on a period and write

$$\|g\|_{2,L}^2:=\frac1L\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx.$$

Elements of $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C)$ are equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define the wave number $\kappa_n:=2\pi n/L$, character $e_n(x):=\exp(i\kappa_n x)$, and Fourier coefficient $\widehat g(n):=L^{-1}\int_0^L g(x)e^{-i\kappa_nx}\,dx$. These formulas are independent of the chosen representative of $x$ in $\mathbb T_L$.

Let $c>0$ be a speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\lambda>0$ be a switching-rate parameter in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. For smooth real initial data $f_{+,0},f_{-,0}$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the two-velocity periodic model is the linear Cauchy problem below; when these functions represent physical densities, also require $f_{\pm,0}\ge0$.

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}.$$

Here $x\in\mathbb T_L$, $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds, and $f_\pm$ have the units of a linear number density, $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The speed magnitude is $c/\epsilon$, and from either velocity state the rate of switching to the opposite state is $\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Define the total density $\rho^\epsilon:=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$, the flux $j^\epsilon:=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$, and the total mass $M^\epsilon(t):=\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every $\epsilon>0$, $c,\lambda,L>0$, and smooth real initial pair $(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the periodic system

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac c\epsilon\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac\lambda{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac c\epsilon\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac\lambda{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}$$

has a unique global smooth solution $(f_+^\epsilon,f_-^\epsilon)$. For a pair $G=(g_+,g_-)$ of square-integrable periodic functions, define $\|G\|_{2,L}^2:=L^{-1}\int_0^L(|g_+|^2+|g_-|^2)\,dx$, and write $F^\epsilon(t):=(f_+^\epsilon(\cdot,t),f_-^\epsilon(\cdot,t))$. Its total mass $M^\epsilon(t)$ is constant. If both initial densities are nonnegative, then both evolved densities are nonnegative. For any two smooth real initial pairs $F_0=(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$ and $G_0=(g_{+,0},g_{-,0})$, denote their solutions by $F^\epsilon$ and $G^\epsilon$; they satisfy

$$\|F^\epsilon(t)-G^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2\le \|F_0-G_0\|_{2,L}^2\qquad(t\ge0),$$

In particular, for one solution,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\|F^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2=-\frac{2\lambda}{\epsilon^2}\|f_+^\epsilon(t)-f_-^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2\le0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Define $j^\epsilon=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$. Adding the two equations in [F1] gives $\partial_t\rho^\epsilon+\partial_xj^\epsilon=0$. Subtracting them and multiplying by $c/\epsilon$ gives $\epsilon^2\partial_tj^\epsilon+2\lambda j^\epsilon=-c^2\partial_x\rho^\epsilon$. The initial condition implies $j^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=0$.

Under [A1], take Fourier coefficients in $x$ in these two identities, with $\kappa_n$ and $\widehat{\cdot}(n)$ from [F1]; differentiate under the compact spatial integral using the smooth solution [F2], and integrate by parts in real and imaginary parts separately using [F4] after the measure-preserving rescaling $y=x/L$. Then $y_n^\epsilon(t):=\widehat{\rho^\epsilon(t)}(n)$ satisfies $\epsilon^2(y_n^\epsilon)''+2\lambda(y_n^\epsilon)'+c^2\kappa_n^2y_n^\epsilon=0$, $y_n^\epsilon(0)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)$, and $(y_n^\epsilon)'(0)=0$. The heat series in the Statement has coefficients $y_n(t)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)e^{-D\kappa_n^2t}$.

Repeated integration by parts in the real and imaginary parts using [F4] gives $\sum_n(1+|\kappa_n|)^r|\widehat{\rho_0}(n)|<\infty$ for every integer $r\ge0$; convergence follows by grouping $2^j\le|n|<2^{j+1}$ after choosing more than $r+1$ derivatives. Therefore the heat series and every differentiated series converge uniformly on compact time intervals, and its coefficient equation $y_n'=-D\kappa_n^2y_n$ proves $\partial_tu=D\partial_x^2u$ with $u(0)=\rho_0$. For any other smooth periodic solution $w$, integration by parts in its Fourier coefficients gives $\widehat w(n)'=-D\kappa_n^2\widehat w(n)$ with initial value $\widehat{\rho_0}(n)$. Multiplying by $e^{D\kappa_n^2t}$ shows that $e^{D\kappa_n^2t}\widehat w(n,t)$ has zero derivative, so $\widehat w(n,t)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)e^{-D\kappa_n^2t}$ for every $n$ and $t$. Fourier completeness [F3] therefore gives $w(t)=u(t)$ as $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L)$ classes for each fixed $t$, hence almost everywhere. Both are continuous in $x$; if they differed at a point, their difference would be bounded away from zero on some nonempty open arc, which has positive normalized Lebesgue measure $dm_L$. This contradicts equality almost everywhere, so $w(t,x)=u(t,x)$ pointwise for every $t,x$.

For $n=0$, the mass mode is constant and equals the heat mode. Fix $n\ne0$. For all sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ with $\epsilon c|\kappa_n|<\lambda$, set $s_n^\epsilon=(-\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^2-\epsilon^2c^2\kappa_n^2})/\epsilon^2$ and $r_n^\epsilon=(-\lambda-\sqrt{\lambda^2-\epsilon^2c^2\kappa_n^2})/\epsilon^2$. The solution of the scalar mode equation is $y_n^\epsilon(t)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)\bigl(A_n^\epsilon e^{s_n^\epsilon t}+B_n^\epsilon e^{r_n^\epsilon t}\bigr)$, where $A_n^\epsilon=\frac12\bigl(1+\lambda/\sqrt{\lambda^2-\epsilon^2c^2\kappa_n^2}\bigr)$ and $B_n^\epsilon=\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda/\sqrt{\lambda^2-\epsilon^2c^2\kappa_n^2}\bigr)$; these coefficients solve $A+B=1$ and $As+Br=0$. Rationalizing the slow root gives $s_n^\epsilon=-c^2\kappa_n^2/(\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^2-\epsilon^2c^2\kappa_n^2})\to-D\kappa_n^2$, while $r_n^\epsilon\to-\infty$, $A_n^\epsilon\to1$, and $B_n^\epsilon\to0$. Put $q=D\kappa_n^2\ge0$; both $s_n^\epsilon$ and $-q$ are nonpositive, so integrating the derivative of $s\mapsto e^{st}$ with [F4] gives $|e^{s_n^\epsilon t}-e^{-qt}|\le t|s_n^\epsilon+q|\le T|s_n^\epsilon+q|$ on $[0,T]$. Since both exponentials have modulus at most one, $|A_n^\epsilon e^{s_n^\epsilon t}+B_n^\epsilon e^{r_n^\epsilon t}-e^{-qt}|\le|A_n^\epsilon-1|+T|s_n^\epsilon+q|+|B_n^\epsilon|$. The right side tends to zero independently of $t\in[0,T]$, proving uniform convergence of this Fourier mode.

Let $P_{>K}$ denote the Fourier projection onto $|n|>K$, applied componentwise to pairs. The mode equations from step 2.1 are decoupled, so the projected pair solves the same system with initial pair $P_{>K}(\rho_0/2,\rho_0/2)$; uniqueness in [F2] identifies it with that evolution. Applying [F2] gives $\|P_{>K}(f_+^\epsilon,f_-^\epsilon)(t)\|_{2,L}\le\|P_{>K}(\rho_0/2,\rho_0/2)\|_{2,L}=\|P_{>K}\rho_0\|_{2,L}/\sqrt2$. Since $\|a+b\|_{2,L}^2\le2(\|a\|_{2,L}^2+\|b\|_{2,L}^2)$, it follows that $\|P_{>K}\rho^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}\le\|P_{>K}\rho_0\|_{2,L}$. The heat multiplier has modulus at most one, hence $\|P_{>K}u(t)\|_{2,L}\le\|P_{>K}\rho_0\|_{2,L}$.

By Parseval [F3], $\|P_{>K}\rho_0\|_{2,L}\to0$ as $K\to\infty$. Given $\eta>0$, choose $K$ so that twice this tail is below $\eta/2$. The finitely many modes $|n|\le K$ converge uniformly on $[0,T]$ by step 3.2, so for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$ their combined $L^2$ error is below $\eta/2$. Step 3.3 bounds the remaining density difference by twice the chosen tail, uniformly in $t$ and $\epsilon$. Therefore $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|\rho^\epsilon(t)-u(t)\|_{2,L}<\eta$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, proving the claim.

For each finite integer $N\ge1$, the phase space is $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ with canonical coordinates $z_i=(q_i,p_i)$, $q_i\in\mathbb T_L^d$ in metres and $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ in kilogram-metres per second. In position charts obtained by lifting torus coordinates to $\mathbb R^d$, define

$$\theta_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d p_i^a\,dq_i^a,\qquad \omega_N:=-d\theta_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_i^a.$$

Overlaps of these position charts are translations by vectors in $L\mathbb Z^d$, with the same momentum coordinates, so $dq_i^a$ and $p_i^a$ agree on overlaps. Thus the displayed forms glue globally on $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$; $\omega_N$ is closed and nondegenerate by its displayed coordinate matrix. Both forms have action units of joule-seconds. Use the Hamiltonian convention $\iota_{X_{H_N}}\omega_N=dH_N$ of [[def-csm-dk-hamiltonian-flow-measure]]. The finite-particle Hamiltonian, with energy in joules, is

$$H_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+\frac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}W(q_i-q_j).$$

The interaction force is $K(q):=-\nabla_qW(q)$, in newtons. It is bounded and globally Lipschitz on the compact torus; evenness of $W$ makes $K$ odd and $K(0)=0$. Hamilton's equations in the canonical convention are

$$\dot q_i=\frac{p_i}{m},\qquad \dot p_i=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}K(q_i-q_j).$$

For any chosen momentum scale $P_0>0$ in kilogram-metres per second, define the time scale $\tau_0:=mL/P_0$ in seconds, dimensionless variables $x_i:=q_i/L\in\mathbb T^d:=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$, $v_i:=p_i/P_0$, and $s:=t/\tau_0$. Define the dimensionless potential $\Phi(x):=mW(Lx)/P_0^2$ and force $k(x):=-\nabla_x\Phi(x)$. Then the equations become

$$x_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}k(x_i-x_j),$$

where prime denotes derivative with respect to dimensionless time $s$. Here
$\|Dk\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^d}\|Dk(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, with operator
norm induced by the Euclidean norm, and $\|k\|_\infty:=\sup_x|k(x)|$; the
constants $A:=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $B:=\|k\|_\infty$ are finite and
dimensionless. This is the selected smooth periodic mean-field scaling; it is
not the hard-sphere Boltzmann-Grad scaling.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge2$, a period length $L>0$ metres, and an equal particle mass $m>0$ kilograms. The position space is the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$. For lifts $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ of points $[x],[y]\in\mathbb T_L^d$, define

$$\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}([x],[y]):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}|x-y+Lk|,$$

where $|z|=(\sum_{\ell=1}^d z_\ell^2)^{1/2}$ is the Euclidean norm. For $q_i=[x]$ and $q_j=[y]$, the vectors $x-y+Lk$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, are the displacement representatives from $q_j$ to $q_i$. The minimum is attained because $|x-y+Lk|\to\infty$ as $|k|\to\infty$, and its value is independent of the chosen lifts because changing lifts reindexes $k$. For each $N\ge2$ under consideration, let $\delta_N>0$ be the physical sphere diameter in metres and put $a_N:=\delta_N/L$. An admissible configuration $(q_1,\ldots,q_N)$ has pairwise distances $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i,q_j)>\delta_N$. For a hard-sphere trajectory below, require $\delta_N<L/2$; this restriction holds eventually in the scaling prescription. If two quotient displacement representatives of length $\delta_N$ existed, their difference would be a nonzero vector in $L\mathbb Z^d$, of length at least $L$, but the triangle inequality bounds its length by $2\delta_N<L$; thus the contact normal is unique.

A hard-sphere trajectory, when defined, is specified on one interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with time $t\in I$ measured in seconds. For each $i=1,\ldots,N$ its maps are
$$q_i:I\longrightarrow\mathbb T_L^d,\qquad v_i:I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,$$
where $v_i$ is measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Require $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t),q_j(t))\ge\delta_N$ for every $t\in I$ and $i\ne j$. The interval may be bounded or unbounded and may include either finite endpoint. Positions are continuous on $I$. Define the interior contact-time set

$$C:=\{t\in I^\circ:\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t),q_j(t))=\delta_N\text{ for some }i<j\}.$$

Require $C$ to be locally finite in $I^\circ$: every compact interval $[a,b]\subset I^\circ$ contains only finitely many elements of $C$. Each $t_c\in C$ must be a binary contact as defined below. In particular, there is an $\eta>0$ with $(t_c-\eta,t_c+\eta)\subset I^\circ$ and $C\cap(t_c-\eta,t_c+\eta)=\{t_c\}$; this is the meaning of an isolated contact. All pairwise distances are strictly greater than $\delta_N$ at interior times outside $C$. A free-flight interval is a maximal open subinterval of $I^\circ$ containing no point of $C$. On each such interval require every $q_i$ and $v_i$ to be $C^1$ and to satisfy $\dot q_i=v_i$ and $\dot v_i=0$. Here $\dot q_i=v_i$ means that any local Euclidean lift of $q_i$ has derivative $v_i$; changing that lift by a constant lattice vector leaves the derivative unchanged.

At an interior contact time use both one-sided velocity limits and set $v_i(t_c)=v_i^+$, the outgoing value. A finite endpoint is included only when the corresponding limits from within $I$ exist, and the position and velocity maps take those values there. No collision rule involving a missing side of an endpoint is imposed; a two-sided update there would require an extension of the trajectory through that time. Contact times may accumulate only at endpoints of $I$ or at infinity; included finite endpoints still require the stated one-sided limits. These conventions specify a partial trajectory only and assert no continuation through a collision accumulation. A binary contact of particles $i,j$ at an interior time $t_c\in I^\circ$ means $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T_L^d}(q_i(t_c),q_j(t_c))=\delta_N$, while no other pair is in contact at $t_c$. Write $v_i^-$ and $v_i^+$ for the one-sided velocity limits at the contact. Let $n$ be the unique unit vector from the centre of $j$ to the centre of $i$ along the shortest quotient displacement. All particles other than $i,j$ retain their velocities at this contact. The equal-mass elastic reflection rule is

$$v_i^+=v_i^- -\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n,\qquad v_j^+=v_j^- +\bigl((v_i^--v_j^-)\cdot n\bigr)n.$$

The Boltzmann–Grad scaling prescription is a sequence, indexed by all sufficiently large integers $N$, with $N\to\infty$, $a_N\to0$, and

$$N a_N^{d-1}=\kappa$$

for a fixed dimensionless $\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Under this exact relation, $a_N=(\kappa/N)^{1/(d-1)}\to0$, so the trajectory restriction $\delta_N<L/2$ holds for every sufficiently large $N$. The factor $a_N$ is the diameter measured relative to the fixed box length, so the displayed parameter is dimensionless. This is a definition of a finite hard-sphere model and a scaling prescription only; it asserts neither global existence of the hard-sphere flow nor convergence to a Boltzmann equation.

Fix a period $L>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T_L:=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$. A smooth periodic function on $\mathbb T_L$ means an $L$-periodic $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R$. For a periodic measurable function $g$ with $\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx<\infty$, use the normalized spatial measure $dm_L=dx/L$ on a period and write

$$\|g\|_{2,L}^2:=\frac1L\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx.$$

Elements of $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C)$ are equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define the wave number $\kappa_n:=2\pi n/L$, character $e_n(x):=\exp(i\kappa_n x)$, and Fourier coefficient $\widehat g(n):=L^{-1}\int_0^L g(x)e^{-i\kappa_nx}\,dx$. These formulas are independent of the chosen representative of $x$ in $\mathbb T_L$.

Let $c>0$ be a speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\lambda>0$ be a switching-rate parameter in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. For smooth real initial data $f_{+,0},f_{-,0}$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the two-velocity periodic model is the linear Cauchy problem below; when these functions represent physical densities, also require $f_{\pm,0}\ge0$.

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}.$$

Here $x\in\mathbb T_L$, $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds, and $f_\pm$ have the units of a linear number density, $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The speed magnitude is $c/\epsilon$, and from either velocity state the rate of switching to the opposite state is $\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Define the total density $\rho^\epsilon:=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$, the flux $j^\epsilon:=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$, and the total mass $M^\epsilon(t):=\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix $L>0$, $c,\lambda>0$, and a nonnegative $\rho_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L)$. For each $\epsilon>0$, let $(f_+^\epsilon,f_-^\epsilon)$ solve the two-velocity periodic model with well-prepared initial data $f_+^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_-^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=\rho_0/2$, and put $\rho^\epsilon=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$. Let $D:=c^2/(2\lambda)$, which has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and define the heat evolution

$$u(t,x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\widehat{\rho_0}(n)e^{-D\kappa_n^2t}e_n(x).$$

Then $u$ is the smooth periodic solution of $\partial_tu=D\partial_x^2u$ with $u(0)=\rho_0$, and for every finite $T>0$,

$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|\rho^\epsilon(t)-u(t)\|_{2,L}=0.$$

This conclusion concerns only the density of the stated linear two-velocity model with well-prepared data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every $\epsilon>0$, $c,\lambda,L>0$, and smooth real initial pair $(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the periodic system

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac c\epsilon\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac\lambda{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac c\epsilon\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac\lambda{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}$$

has a unique global smooth solution $(f_+^\epsilon,f_-^\epsilon)$. For a pair $G=(g_+,g_-)$ of square-integrable periodic functions, define $\|G\|_{2,L}^2:=L^{-1}\int_0^L(|g_+|^2+|g_-|^2)\,dx$, and write $F^\epsilon(t):=(f_+^\epsilon(\cdot,t),f_-^\epsilon(\cdot,t))$. Its total mass $M^\epsilon(t)$ is constant. If both initial densities are nonnegative, then both evolved densities are nonnegative. For any two smooth real initial pairs $F_0=(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$ and $G_0=(g_{+,0},g_{-,0})$, denote their solutions by $F^\epsilon$ and $G^\epsilon$; they satisfy

$$\|F^\epsilon(t)-G^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2\le \|F_0-G_0\|_{2,L}^2\qquad(t\ge0),$$

In particular, for one solution,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\|F^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2=-\frac{2\lambda}{\epsilon^2}\|f_+^\epsilon(t)-f_-^\epsilon(t)\|_{2,L}^2\le0.$$

derivations.claim: The mean-field coefficient $1/N$ and particle number $N$ are dimensionless; $q_i$ has units m, $p_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, $W$ and $H_N$ have units J, and $K=-\nabla W$ has units N by [F1]. The total momentum $P_N=\sum_i p_i$ is conserved because $\dot P_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i<j}(K(q_i-q_j)+K(q_j-q_i))=0$ by oddness of $K$. Along any differentiable Hamiltonian trajectory, $H_N$ is constant: the defining convention $\iota_{X_{H_N}}\omega_N=dH_N$ gives $dH_N(X_{H_N})=\omega_N(X_{H_N},X_{H_N})=0$ since a two-form is antisymmetric. The model keeps the finite particle count $N$ fixed; its separate mean-field scaling varies $N$ while retaining the smooth all-to-all interaction coefficient $1/N$.

In the hard-sphere scaling, $N$ and $a_N=\delta_N/L$ are dimensionless and $a_N=(\kappa/N)^{1/(d-1)}\to0$. Between collisions every velocity is constant. At a binary collision set $U=(v_i^-+v_j^-)/2$ and $g=v_i^--v_j^-$. The rule in [F2] leaves $U$ unchanged and sends $g$ to $g'=g-2(g\cdot n)n$, so $|g'|^2=|g|^2$ because $|n|=1$. Therefore the pair momentum $m(v_i+v_j)=2mU$ and pair kinetic energy $\frac m2(|v_i|^2+|v_j|^2)=m|U|^2+\frac m4|g|^2$ are unchanged. Other particles are unaffected at this isolated binary collision. Thus momentum and kinetic energy are unchanged between any two times across which only finitely many of these collision updates occur, by composing the free-flight and single-collision equalities. This comparison uses only the specified collision rule; it does not assert existence of a global hard-sphere flow or address accumulation of collisions.

For the two-velocity model, $[c/\epsilon]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $[\lambda/\epsilon^2]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ by [F3], so $D=c^2/(2\lambda)$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Its conserved quantity is the total density mass $\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$ by [F5]; the limiting heat equation preserves the same mass because its zero Fourier mode is constant. It has no particle-count parameter $N$, pair potential $W$, hard-sphere diameter $\delta_N$, or collision events.

The three prescriptions constrain different variables and specify different state spaces: a smooth Hamiltonian $N$-body system with $1/N$ pair coupling, a hard-sphere system with $N a_N^{d-1}=\kappa$, and a two-component periodic density equation with $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The conservation checks in steps 1.1–1.3 concern their own equations and collision rule. They supply no cross-family implication or molecular-chaos or hard-sphere derivation of the two-velocity heat equation, so none is claimed here.
